examples: I eat rice in the morning.
nuance: 밥 means both cooked rice and a meal in general. So 밥 먹었어요? often just asks if you have eaten, not only about rice.
mistakes: Thinking 밥 only means rice, never a meal

nuance: In Korean, 국 is eaten with a spoon alongside rice at almost every meal. Koreans say they eat 국 rather than drink it.
mistakes: Using 마셔요 (drink) instead of 먹어요 for 국

examples: This kimchi is a bit spicy.
nuance: 김치 is the most common side dish and appears at nearly every Korean meal. It is usually served free at restaurants and can be refilled.
mistakes: Treating 김치 as a main dish instead of a side dish

examples: I want to eat meat tonight.
nuance: 고기 alone usually means pork or beef in everyday speech. For fish people say 생선, and chicken is often called 닭고기 to be specific.
mistakes: Assuming 고기 includes fish or chicken by default

nuance: 생선 is fish meant for eating, while a live swimming fish is 물고기. Use 생선 at restaurants and markets, not for fish in a pond.
mistakes: Saying 물고기 when ordering fish to eat

examples: I eat a lot of vegetables.
I eat meat and vegetables together.
nuance: 야채 and 채소 both mean vegetables and are often interchangeable. 야채 sounds slightly more casual and is very common in daily conversation.
mistakes: Adding a plural marker because English says vegetables

examples: I buy fruit at the market.
nuance: 과일 is an uncountable group word, so you do not add a plural ending even when talking about many pieces. Name a specific fruit like 사과 when you need to.
mistakes: Trying to make 과일 plural like the English word

examples: I eat an apple every morning.
nuance: 사과 also means an apology, so the same word can mean either depending on context. At a fruit store it clearly means the fruit apple.
mistakes: Confusing 사과 the fruit with 사과 meaning apology

examples: I eat bread in the morning.
I buy bread at the bakery.
nuance: 빵 covers all baked goods including cakes and pastries, not just plain loaves. A bakery is called 빵집, literally a bread house.
mistakes: Limiting 빵 to only sliced loaf bread

examples: I drink a glass of milk in the morning.
nuance: 우유 is a drink, so it takes 마셔요 (drink), not 먹어요 (eat). It refers to plain cow milk unless you add a word like 딸기 for strawberry.
mistakes: Using 먹어요 instead of 마셔요 with 우유

examples: We eat lunch at the restaurant.
Let us go to that restaurant.
nuance: 식당 takes 에서 for an action done inside it but 에 when it is only the destination. 식당 is a casual eatery, while a fancier place may be called 레스토랑.
mistakes: Using 에 instead of 에서 for eating at a place

examples: This restaurant has many menu items.
Let us look at the menu together.
nuance: 메뉴 means both the list of dishes and a single dish you order. Asking 무슨 메뉴 먹을까요? means which dish should we get.
mistakes: Thinking 메뉴 only means the printed list, not a dish
